newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Inflation, tax goals seen hard for Portugal in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Inflation, tax goals seen hard for Portugal in 1997.

text.p: Economists saluted the draft 1997 budget presented by Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco on Friday but said inflation and projected tax revenues posed some problems.
The predicted 2.25 to 2.5 percent inflation rate depends on the government holding the line on salaries, they said.
The projected nine percent rise in tax income could be tough if the government sticks rigidly to its pledge not to raise overall tax levels, they added.

Four economists polled by Reuters after the finance ministry released some budget data for 1997 felt the target of a 2.9 percent budget deficit to GDP ratio could be achieved but it would be difficult.
Hitting the target is vital to Portugal's hopes of being in the firve of European countries moving to monetary union.
"The budget has its eyes fixed on Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), but the doubts are over inflation and tax receipts," said one investment bank analyst who asked not to be named.
"Wage moderation...is going to be a real test for the government," echoed analyst Jose Luis Alzola of Salomon Brothers.

"With the (budget) information that we have, which is not that much, the estimates for tax receipts could be somewhat optimistic. They are hoping for significant improvements in fiscal efficiency," he added.

Analyst Carlo Rebelo of Lisbon's Finantia also felt that achieving a rise in tax income, without increasing in tax rates, of nine percent when the economy was only expected to rise some 5.0-5.5 percent in nominal terms could be hard.
The government's deficit/GDP target is just inside the three percent ceiling set for EMU entry. The ratio should be around four percent this year.
The economy is expected to grow around three percent next year, slightly above this year's rate.
